1:
Three voices open by fixing the sermon's extent, and none stops at the chapter. Keil and Delitzsch divide the discourse into three sections, the first running into the opening verses of the next chapter, and give its argument in advance: from the people's reliance on the possession of the temple and the legal sacrificial worship, the prophet turns to the destruction of Shiloh to show that Jerusalem will not escape the fate of the northern kingdom. Ellicott takes this chapter and the three that follow as one great sermon delivered to the crowds that flocked to the Temple.

On the date they differ in confidence. Clarke supposes the first year of Jehoiakim, who, far from following his pious father, restored idolatry and maintained bad priests and worse prophets. Ellicott finds nothing that absolutely fixes a date, but reads the prevalence of idolatry, and possibly a reference to the invader already at hand, as fitting Jehoiakim's reign rather than Josiah's; and since a later chapter reports a Shiloh prophecy from the beginning of that reign, he thinks it probably this discourse, or one like it, that drew down the king's displeasure.

The gate divides them four ways. Gill reports from a Jewish commentator the eastern gate, the principal of them all, and Wesley agrees, calling it the public place of going out and coming in, where the people were wont to assemble. Ellicott, noting that a priest had access to every part of the building, places him at the inner gate of one of the courts, possibly the one by which the king entered in state, looking out over the multitudes that thronged it. Keil and Delitzsch leave the choice among the three gates of the inner court open, suggesting the one where Baruch afterwards read the prophecies aloud.

On the occasion they converge. Keil and Delitzsch argue from the form of address, all Judah, ye that enter in, that it was one of the great annual festivals, the people gathering from the length and breadth of the land; Henry supposes one of the three feasts, when the men of the whole country appeared before God and none empty; Calvin reaches it from the other side, that on ordinary days only the inhabitants of the city frequented the courts.

Amending the ways is taken for more than mending conduct. Keil and Delitzsch make the verb mean to make one's way good, that is, to lead a good life, and separate the terms, the ways being the tendency of life at large and the doings its individual manifestations; Ellicott divides them the same way, general habits against separate acts. Henry requires a reformation universal, constant and sincere rather than partial or hypocritical, since the tree must be made good to make the fruit good, the heart amended so that the ways may be. Calvin makes this the sermon's whole object: after the feast every man went home as though, having made his expiation, he had God propitious to him, and the answer is that God does not regard the external rites at all.

The promise attached to it is disputed in the translating. Ellicott warns that the English suggests something new when the words offer only the continuance of blessings already enjoyed, and renders it I will let you dwell. Calvin prefers the verb read the other way, I will dwell with you in this place, following the older versions and arguing from the context, since their boast was that God dwelt among them because the house was his. He hears an implied contrast, that the people would not long survive unless they sought another way to pacify God. Keil and Delitzsch keep the plainer sense, that only good endeavours give a sure title to a long lease of the land, while Gill grounds the demand in the title of hosts, armies above and below.
4:
Why the temple is named three times over is the first question, and four answers are given. Clarke reports the Chaldee paraphrase, which turns the clause into a liturgy — before the temple ye shall worship, before the temple ye shall sacrifice, thrice in the year ye shall appear — and says the Targumist supposed this the reason for the repetition; he himself thinks the words rather express the people's conviction that they were safe while the temple service continued, God not being likely to give it up into profane hands. Ellicott hears the burden of the false prophets' discourses, and possibly the solemn iteration of the words in the supplicants' litanies, a people harping on the building's greatness, identifying themselves with it and predicting its perpetuity while giving no thought to the presence it symbolised.

Calvin claims to supply what interpreters have omitted. Taking these of the three parts, the court, the holy place and the innermost, he makes the repetition a triple defence: a city walled not once but three times is thought impregnable, and the Jews had set up just such a triple rampart against God's judgments. Wesley takes the plural more simply, of the courts and the house and the holiest, which the prophet in the gate points at as with his finger. Gill notes only that the lying words are the lying prophets' words, and Calvin, canvassing the versions, records that several of the older ones give the phrase twice rather than thrice and put the verb in the singular.

On the condition itself the demand is total. Clarke renders it literally, if in making good ye fully make good your ways, and says God will no longer admit half-hearted work: semblances of piety cannot deceive him and he will not accept a partial reformation. Gill refers the amendment to the duties of the moral law, more acceptable to God than legal sacrifices when done from love, in faith, and to his glory. Keil and Delitzsch narrow the justice required, since the added phrase shows the point is helping one man to his rights against another, the law having attached penalties to the oppression of those who most needed protection. Calvin has the prophet address the judges first, requiring judgment without favour or hatred and unmoved by bribes; Ellicott glosses the phrase as the Jewish idiom for one man and another.

The three protected classes are read together. Ellicott groups the stranger, the fatherless and the widow as the great representatives of the poor and helpless, most in need of man's justice and of divine protection; Gill adds that they should not be injured by private men, much less oppressed in the courts by those who ought to be their patrons and defenders; Calvin makes their treatment the test of a government, since where others obtain their right it is no wonder, having advocates and friends, but justice done to these is evidence of real integrity. Wesley counts three sins in the verse, oppression, blood and idolatry, and observes that the instance chosen is the worst of oppressions.

Two smaller readings close it. Ellicott notes that the English punctuation attaches the words about perpetuity to the promise of dwelling while the Hebrew accentuation attaches them to the gift made to the fathers, intended to last but forfeited by the people's guilt; Calvin connects them with the verb instead, so that they remain from age to age as their fathers did. On the words that cannot profit Gill observes the note of asseveration, that what they were dissuaded from is now affirmed of them; and Calvin makes the falsehood an impious divorce, since the sacrifices were meant to show men they deserved death and to send them for mercy, and to lay hold on the naked sign while overlooking the reality turns the institution to a contrary end.
9:
The catalogue of crimes is first a matter of grammar. Ellicott says the English obscures the emphasis of the idiom, which gives the verbs as infinitives: What, to steal, to murder, to burn incense to Baal, and then have ye come before me. Keil and Delitzsch read the query before them as wonder and indignation, and count the breaches, three commandments of the second table and then two of the first; the clause about gods they knew not they set against the opening of the law, since those gods had never made themselves known in benefits. Gill divides the list the same way. Calvin turns the grammar into an accusation: men who take sacrifices out of their plunder to expiate their crimes make God a participator in the robbery.

What the worshippers then said divides them. Ellicott notes that a different pointing yields Deliver us, reproducing the people's own prayer with indignant scorn; keeping the word as it stands, he has them passing between the two worships and leaving the fast feeling they were saved, and hears the prophet repeat it ironically, delivered not from their abominations but as if set free to do them. Calvin agrees they never said it in words, and reports a version rendering it a petition before preferring the declarative sense. Wesley puts it plainly, that having appeared with their sacrifices they thought themselves privileged to return to their wickedness.

Two voices work the den of robbers into the same shape. Ellicott gives the geography, a country whose limestone caves had always sheltered outlaws, and says those who thronged the courts, priests and prophets among them, were such robbers, soothing their consciences by their worship. Calvin gives the logic: robbers dare not use the sword in the open for fear of the laws, and take their liberty only where they are hidden, so that had there been no temple some integrity might have survived on common feeling alone. Keil and Delitzsch fix the phrase in your eyes to the verb, making it a question whether they so took it, and answer that men who gathered there for absolution were in the very act declaring it a robbers' retreat.

Shiloh is the agreed precedent, disputed in its details. Clarke has God let the sanctuary fall to the Philistines and be set up in the house of their idols, for the iniquity of the priests and the people. Ellicott insists the place had never been a centre of light and purity, defiled by half-idolatrous dances, by shameless violence and by the sins of the priest's sons, and suggests that buildings had gathered round the tabernacle whose ruins gave the allusion its force; he adds that this reference, more than anything else in the sermon, provoked the wrath of priest and people, who had thought with half-concealed exultation of the fall of the northern sanctuary that gave way to their own. Keil and Delitzsch admit there is no historical notice of the event and read the command to go and look as rhetoric strengthening the threat, since sacredness does not save a place from overthrow. Gill says the going is not local but a taking of the place into the mind.

Calvin disputes which ruin is meant, preferring the desolation that followed the removal of the ark to the later devastation of the northern captivity, since only the earlier makes the argument complete; and presses the words about the first setting of the name, so that Shiloh is not merely equal in privilege but excels in antiquity. On rising early Ellicott observes that the phrase belongs to this prophet alone and in its bold anthropomorphism takes the highest form of human activity, waking from sleep and beginning at dawn, to picture the like in God; Calvin reads it as a father's care, God claiming as his own the labour done through his prophets.
16:
The ban on praying is a hard word, answered four ways. Ellicott takes it that an intercession like Moses' was already rising in the prophet's heart and had to be checked, since judgment must have its way and the discipline do its work; the conflict between his human affections and the divine will, he adds, made the sentence more terrible than ever. Henry reads the prohibition as evidence of prayer's weight, God bespeaking his prophet beforehand because he would not have such prayers lie unanswered, and calls it an ill omen when the spirits of ministers are restrained from praying for a people. Calvin makes it a mercy to the prophet, who had not divested himself of human feelings and might have been tardier in denouncing vengeance had pity been left to melt him. Clarke asks how terrible a place must be where God refuses the spirit of supplication on its behalf. Wesley alone qualifies the ban, holding that the prophet certainly did pray for a remnant, though not for the revoking of the decree.

The household at its work is described alike and turned to the same use. Clarke lays out the division of labour, the children collecting wood, the fathers kindling the fire, the mother and her maids kneading and baking, and ends in reproach: what a pity so few families show such zeal in the worship of God. Henry draws the same lesson, that we should be as diligent in teaching our children the truths of God as many are in teaching the mysteries of iniquity. Calvin gives the young the wood as the heavier work, and finds in the completeness of it an insane rivalry in which no part was neglected; Gill agrees they were not little children but young men able to fell trees.

Who was worshipped is less settled. Ellicott identifies a kind of Assyrian Artemis, joined to the moon and to the symbolic worship of the reproductive powers of nature, whose ritual probably resembled the Babylonian one in its impurities, and distinguishes her from Ashtoreth, whose name signifies a star and belongs to another planet. Clarke and Wesley take the moon, Clarke allowing that the sun and planets may not be excluded and Wesley setting the sun as king against the moon as queen. Calvin will not settle it: a missing letter would give the workmanship of the heavens rather than a queen, and he lets every man enjoy his own opinion, inclining to the moon if the title stands.

Whether God is provoked at all draws careful answers. Gill denies the affection outright, since there is no such perturbation in God as in men, and though he does what men do in anger the damage of sin falls on the sinner. Keil and Delitzsch reach it through the grammar, taking the pronoun reflexively, so that instead of vexing him they vex themselves, the consequences of their idolatry falling on their own head. Calvin says he could be without their worship and suffer no loss, and that their fury returns upon them. Ellicott objects to the translators, whose supplied words complete the sense but mar the abrupt force of the original: is it not themselves, to the confusion of their own faces?

The pouring out of the fury closes it. Ellicott traces the verb, used elsewhere of a plague of rain and here of a great shower of fire, and notes it had been on Josiah's lips when he heard the judgments denounced in the newly found book of the law. Calvin asks why the sentence reaches innocent beasts and trees and fruit, and answers that the world was made for man, so the symptoms of wrath are extended through all the elements to show how displeased God is with him. Wesley observes only that the unquenchable fire shows the resolution is not to be revoked.
21:
The command to pile the offerings up and eat is taken as irony, each rendering the sarcasm differently. Henry has God tell them to turn the whole burnt offering into a peace offering they may dine on, since a good meal's meat or two is all the good they are likely to get by it, and reports another reading, keep your sacrifices to yourselves and let them be served at your own table, for they are no way acceptable at God's altar. Clarke makes it plain refusal, that neither sacrifice nor oblation will be received, so the beasts set apart may as well be slain for common nourishment. Ellicott keeps it shorter, add one kind to another and partake of the feast, all fruitless without repentance and holiness. Calvin hears God excluding himself, ye sacrifice to yourselves and not to me, and notes that the verb may come from a root meaning to sweep together, which suits the contempt better. Wesley says only that they may do what they will with what was peculiar to God, who will have none of it.

The harder saying is that nothing was commanded about offerings at the coming out of Egypt, and four voices reconcile it. Ellicott presses the preposition, literally with a view to, and argues that sacrifice was never the end contemplated: the first promulgation of the law set out a spiritual and ethical religion, and the ritual came afterwards, partly as a concession to the temper that had shown itself in the worship of the calf and partly as an education. Henry reaches it from the order of the books, the moral precepts standing before the ceremonial, and observes that the sacrificial law opens as though it meant rather to regulate sacrifice than to require it. Wesley makes the denial comparative, the offerings condemned not in themselves but against obedience. Calvin grants the objection full force, since the sacrifices promoted penitence and were pledges of expiation, and answers that the prophet speaks to the ideas of men who had vitiated them: God joined the sign to its end, and it is not in man's power to separate what he has connected.

Gill supplies the aggravation, that a people bound to serve by creation and by providence were bound further by the distinguishing blessings of goodness, so their sins were the more heinous. Keil and Delitzsch put the failure in a phrase, that they neglected what was foremost and cardinal in the law, and note that the two words for their walking stand in apposition rather than subordination; the Greek could not admit this and dropped the second, and several critics have followed it in deleting the word as a gloss.

Going backward rather than forward is read three ways. Clarke counts the descent in four steps, from not hearkening, to not inclining the ear, to walking after an evil heart's motions, to a decline that left them more profligate than their fathers. Calvin fixes on the resolve rather than the drift, since they not only followed their own ways but made resolutions to walk in them, and leaves them no excuse but the wish to be wiser than God. Ellicott takes the phrase furthest, correcting imagination to stubbornness and judging the whole sacrificial system, even at its best and apart from its corruptions, a retrograde movement away from the first and purely spiritual covenant.

Ellicott closes with an observation no one else makes. The influence of this teaching on later Jewish thought can be measured from the synagogue lectionary, where this passage stands as the lesson from the prophets appointed to follow the sacrificial portion of the law; that service, being in the nature of the case the work of scribes and prophets rather than priests, bore witness to the spiritual truth symbolised in sacrifice and not to the perpetuation of the symbol.
25:
The daily sending of the prophets is agreed, then examined. Wesley states the principle, that the church has never wanted teachers raised up and sent by God. Ellicott presses the history: the stress falls on a continual succession of witnesses from the beginning, and though the prominence given to Samuel as the first to bear the name seems against it, the gift was bestowed freely as early as the wilderness, prophets and men of God appear through the judges, and seers were honoured before Samuel, so that what was new in his ministry was the name and the organisation rather than the gift. Calvin reads the daily rising as God's persistence across generations, the children succeeding their fathers in the same corruptions until the imitation became perpetual. Gill notes only that the disobedience runs from the first coming out of Egypt.

That they did worse than their fathers raises a question of measure. Ellicott finds the survey too rapid to say whether the comparison lies between the generation that came out and their immediate followers or between those and their successors, and settles for the thought that the whole history had been one of progressive deterioration climaxing in the prophet's own time; he sets beside it a Roman historian's complaint and the poet's line about a fathers' age more stained with crime than their sires, bringing forth a later race yet more base. Calvin cares less for the degree than for the plea it supports: descent from corrupt fathers looks like an extenuation, and is urged as one by those who plead antiquity, but continued indulgence in vice does not serve for a precedent, and the dead are joined to the living precisely to make the guilt twofold.

The commission that follows is hard, and its grammar worked over. Ellicott would render both clauses concessively, though thou shalt speak, yet they will not hearken; though thou shalt call, yet they will not answer. Keil and Delitzsch get the same sense out of the consecutive form, which reads literally speak to them and they will not hearken, meaning even if thou speakest. Calvin finds the indignation in the change of person, since God had said your fathers and I sent unto you and now says they hearkened not, as one wearied with addressing a stupid people and turning to speak of them instead. He weighs what it cost, since the prophets did not divest themselves of human affections and loved their own nation, yet that sorrow did not keep them from executing their office boldly; ministers now, he adds, must follow their course even where the doctrine proves a savour of death.

What remains is not teaching but sentence. Calvin marks the change of manner: the first duty of teachers is to set forth God's will and then exhort, and here, after long trial, the prophet is bidden not to address them but to pronounce on them, that the world might know how base their obstinacy had been; he adds that the word for nation is the one Scripture sets against the chosen people, so the Jews might learn they were of the same class as the rest. Keil and Delitzsch quote an older commentator to the same effect, that the words are to be said even to those who will not obey, so they may know what they are and what awaits them, and observe that faithfulness is cut off out of their mouth rather than the heart because their profession never stopped. Ellicott sharpens the article, this is the nation, pre-eminent in its sin, and corrects truth to faithfulness. Clarke sums it as a loss of both means, since blessings and corrections have been equally thrown away; Wesley puts it shortest, that there is no believing them in anything they say. Gill dates the verdict to experience, after long speaking and calling.
29:
The shorn hair is read by all as the Nazarite's. Ellicott supplies the philology, the word meaning a crown or diadem and being the one applied to the unshorn locks from which the Nazarite took his name; as he had to shave on touching a corpse, and close cutting was among these peoples the sign of extremest sorrow, the city is to sit as a woman put away and bereaved of her children. Henry turns it into a sentence: Jerusalem had been a Nazarite to God, and must now be separated from him as she had been separated to him, for it is time that those who have lost their holiness should lay aside their joy. Clarke makes it a command to drop the pretence and throw off the mask, and reports another scholar's view that the prophet himself is addressed, a Nazarite by office, before rejecting it as less natural. Gill and Calvin settle that point from the feminine verb, Calvin refusing an emendation that changes the gender through the verse without warrant of manuscript or version.

The abominations in the house are traced two ways. Ellicott gives the history, the thing done by Ahaz, repeated by Manasseh after the cleansing, checked by Josiah, and quite possibly swinging back when that king's death left the idolatrous party free. Calvin gives the offence, that bringing idols into God's very presence was a literal breach of the first commandment, and that the evasion used is the one still used, that images are helps to devotion. Henry hears defiance in it, as though they would reconcile heaven and hell in one court.

The name of Tophet draws the most detailed work. Gill and Wesley report the derivation from a drum, beaten so the parents might not hear the children's cries. Ellicott canvasses that etymology with a garden and a place of burning, thinks the drum may be original, but prefers to treat the word as no local name at all: it appears elsewhere for a thing spat upon, so the prophets have substituted it for Baal in contempt, and a later repetition of this prediction says the high places of Baal outright. Calvin notes that both names came to stand for the infernal regions, and presses the geography, since the place lay in the suburbs within sight of the temple, so their guilt was the greater.

The sentence makes the place of the sin the place of the punishment. Keil and Delitzsch put it plainly, that where they sacrificed their children they shall themselves be massacred and buried in that unclean ground for want of room. Ellicott corrects the English to because there is no room, and observes that the dead will be laid where both parties would have avoided burying, sacred to the one and accursed to the other. Calvin adds the legal difficulty, that a corpse defiled and no sacrifice might be offered near a grave, so consecrating that place had been a profanation from the first; and defends burial as a custom held sacred in all ages and a symbol of the resurrection.

The silencing of the marriages closes it. Keil and Delitzsch read the voice of bridegroom and bride as a circumlocution for the mirth of the wedding feast, all of it now dumb. Calvin takes it as a part for the whole, since without marriages the race cannot continue, so what ceases is all that holds society together. Ellicott finds the imagery characteristic and says nothing could paint the break-up of a nation's life more forcibly, wailing giving way to something worse, the utter silence of solitude; the word for waste, he notes, is used only of places once inhabited and fallen into ruin. Clarke ends on the proportion: such sins required such a punishment, and must be horrible indeed when they move God to destroy the work of his own hands.
